topic_tag: stones in a steep river's bed
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Their report argued that the river had ______ those stones, and its photographs set out the case.

worlds.passage: Two geologists measured the stones of a steep river running eight miles from granite and sandstone cliffs to the sea. Their report argued that the river had ______ those stones, and its photographs set out the case. Sieved, the bed held oven-sized boulders at the cliffs, fist-sized cobbles midway, and pea gravel at the sea. Painted stones turned up, flood by flood, wherever the bed held stones their own size. Below a spring that runs orange, the stones are orange too, the color running clear through any stone cracked open. At the mouth, in water gray with grit, broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge.
worlds.explanation: Each stretch of the river held stones of nearly one size, and painted stones traveled with each flood to wherever the bed held stones their own size, so the river had separated its stones by size along its course: it had "sorted" them. "Stacked" means set one on another, but the painted stones moved on with every flood. "Stained" means colored from outside, and the spring does run orange, but the orange runs clear through any stone cracked open, so it is the rock's own color. "Sanded" means worn down by grit, and the river at the mouth carries grit, but broken pebbles there still fit back together edge to edge.

stacked.why: Stacked stones are set firmly on one another; these were carried on with every flood.
stacked.surface_fit: Rivers lean and pile their stones on one another, and a report on how a river arranged its bed could easily say stacked.
stacked.inference: stones that move on with each flood until they reach the stretch of their own size are never left resting on or braced against one another, so the river was moving them, not setting them one upon another

stained.quote: the color running clear through any stone cracked open
stained.why: Staining colors a surface from outside; the orange runs through the whole stone, so it is the rock's own color.
stained.surface_fit: A spring runs orange and the stones below it are orange too, which looks exactly like water staining the stones.
stained.inference: a stain from the spring would coat the outside, but these stones are orange all the way through, so the color is the rock's own and the spring did not put it there

sanded.quote: broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge
sanded.why: Sanded stones are worn at their edges; these broken edges had lost nothing.
sanded.surface_fit: At the mouth the water is gray with grit, the very abrasive that sands stones smooth.
sanded.inference: even where the water carries grit, broken halves still fit edge to edge, so the grit had not worn the stones at all

worlds.passage: Two geologists measured the stones of a steep river running eight miles from granite and sandstone cliffs to the sea. Their report argued that the river had ______ those stones, and its photographs set out the case. Sieved, the bed held the same mix of sizes at the cliffs as at the sea. The flat stones all tilted one way, each leaning on its downstream neighbor, and painted ones stayed put through five spring floods. A stone cracked open showed the same shade inside as out. Even at the sea, broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge.
worlds.explanation: The flat stones all tilted one way, each leaning on its downstream neighbor, and stayed in place through five floods, so the river had laid them one upon another: it had "stacked" them. "Sorted" means separated by size, but the sieved mix of sizes was the same at the cliffs as at the sea. "Stained" means given a color from outside, but a cracked stone showed the same shade inside as out. "Sanded" means worn down by grit, but even at the sea broken pebbles still fit back together edge to edge, so their edges had lost nothing.
